name: Poa
look_here_first: BOAT-PROW LEAF TIPS help recognize Poa, but do not distinguish species. INTRODUCED P. annua is generally a small low tuft with bisexual pale green seedheads; native P. arachnifera is a rhizomatous perennial, DIOECIOUS with male and female plants. Female Texas bluegrass spikelets have dense COBWEBBY hairs at the lemma bases; these hairs need real macro proof.

recognition.where_to_look_first: Follow shoot to intact base (tuft vs rhizome); inspect folded boat-tipped leaves and true membranous ligule; check flowerhead size/color as preliminary clue; inspect mature lemma base/flower sex under microscope for Texas bluegrass.
priority: small mostly annual tuft vs persistent rhizomatous sod
boat-shaped leaf tips (both!) and membranous true ligules

comparison_lesson.title: Poa annual bluegrass versus Texas bluegrass
comparison_lesson.memory_rule: BOTH have BOAT TIPS. Tiny greener introduced tuft / bisexual P. annua vs native rhizomatous Texas bluegrass with SEPARATE SEXES and FEMALE WEBBY LEMMAS.
quick_split: INTRODUCED annual bluegrass: soft low light-green grass in lawns and paths with small open pale green panicles; folded emerging blades with boat-prow tips and a translucent short membranous ligule. Usually annual, though persistent biotypes occur. True flowers are generally bisexual, unlike dioecious Texas bluegrass.

Native TEXAS BLUEGRASS is a rhizomatous sod-forming cool-season PERENNIAL, dioecious with male and female plants. Female spikelet florets have conspicuous cobwebby long hairs at basal lemmas that make whole flowering heads look woolly. A distant fuzzy head is only a clue: a verified female floret macro and rooted rhizomes are needed.
comparison_lesson.guardrail: Do not mistake a fuzzy distant panicle for microscopically verified webby female floret hairs; P. annua sometimes persists as perennial biotypes.

field_traits: Cool-season generally annual; persistent biotypes can occur in managed moist turf.
Low flowering tuft with small spreading greenish seedheads; can flower under close mowing.
Young folded blades have prow-like boat-shaped tips; this is a genus clue NOT species-specific.
Ligule membranous around 0.5–3 mm according to Williamson County treatment; no auricles.
Spikelets commonly with bisexual florets; unlike separate-sex Texas bluegrass.
comparisons.lookalike_caution: P. arachnifera is a rhizomatous native perennial, often taller in spring prairie/open-oak habitat, with separate male and female plants. Female heads can appear cobwebby because of dense fine hairs at lemma bases. P. annua is typically a small introduced flowering tuft whose flowerheads are pale green and have bisexual florets. Both have boat tips, so inspect whole root system and florets.

field_traits: Perennial spreading on underground rhizomes forming prairie grass sod, often 20–70 cm high.
Dioecious: male and female florets on separate individuals.
Female spikelets have strongly woolly/cobwebby basal lemma hair tufts; 20× image essential.
Bright to pale silver flowering heads in spring and smooth sheaths.
Boat-shaped blade tips and a membranous true ligule are genus-level characteristics.
comparisons.lookalike_caution: Introduced P. annua commonly forms a small shorter-lived tuft with often open triangular green flowering panicles containing bisexual flowers. Texas bluegrass spreads through persistent rhizomes and displays dioecious sex-specific heads; female florets have dense webby hairs at lemma bases. Full panicle color/texture alone is inadequate for ID.

what_to_teach_crew: Poa boat-prow leaf tips are shared, not diagnostic for individual species.
Rhizomes, full flowering stature, plant sex and individual lemma-base hairs are needed.
No microbiological claim from a landscape photograph.
Native Hays County planting metrics not changed by this genus photo pass.
